title: Secure Software Development Lifecycle
summary: The Secure Software Development Lifecycle is a structured way of weaving security activities into every phase of how software is planned, built, tested, released and maintained, rather than bolting security on at the end. In a mature SSDLC, requirements work establishes abuse cases and security acceptance criteria alongside functional ones, design work produces threat models and data-flow diagrams, implementation follows approved patterns and hardened libraries, verification combines static analysis, dependency review and dynamic testing, and release gates confirm that findings are triaged and that artifacts are signed. Operations closes the loop through monitoring, vulnerability intake and a defined patch cadence. For a practising security engineer the importance of the SSDLC is organisational rather than technical: it converts a series of ad hoc code reviews into a repeatable set of gates with named owners, entry and exit criteria, and evidence. That evidence is what makes the process auditable and what lets a security team argue for design-time intervention instead of endless reactive reviews. Typical failure modes are well known. Security work is defined as a gate rather than a service, so developers route around it. Threat models are produced once and never revisited when architecture changes. Tooling generates thousands of findings with no triage SLA, producing alert fatigue and eventual ignoring of the whole pipeline. Exceptions are granted verbally and never expire. The strongest programmes measure how early defects are caught and how quickly accepted risks are revisited, and they treat a blocked release as a process defect to be fixed, not a hero moment.
objectives: You will be able to describe the phases of a secure development lifecycle and name the security activities that belong in each.
You will be able to write security acceptance criteria and abuse cases that are testable by engineering teams.
You will be able to design proportionate release gates that block on high-severity findings without paralysing delivery.
You will be able to explain how threat modelling, static analysis, dependency review and dynamic testing complement each other and where each is blind.
You will be able to define a vulnerability triage workflow with severity mapping, owners, SLAs and expiry-bound exceptions.
You will be able to evaluate whether an SSDLC programme is genuinely embedded or merely documented, using observable evidence.
